name: GLOW Blend (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu)

b.x: At least 4,000 human genes respond to a single copper-binding tripeptide. That tripeptide is GHK-Cu, and the GLOW Blend builds an entire healing protocol around it. Full name: BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu (also called the triple healing stack). No CAS number exists for the combination. BPC-157 upregulates VEGF to build new blood vessels at injury sites. It modulates nitric oxide for vascular protection and activates the FAK-paxillin pathway for tendon and ligament repair. TB-500 (the active fragment of Thymosin Beta-4) upregulates actin, a cell-building protein that moves repair cells to wound sites. Thymosin beta-4 also has anti-inflammatory activity, per a 2016 review [5]. GHK-Cu delivers copper ions to tissue, triggering collagen I and III synthesis and decorin expression for organized (not fibrotic) tissue remodeling. Community adoption sits at roughly 200+ Reddit threads and a 4.3/5 sentiment score. Users consistently describe higher-quality healed tissue compared to BPC-157 plus TB-500 alone, with less scar formation and visible skin improvements by week four. The primary complaint: budget pre-mixed vials deliver roughly 200 mcg of GHK-Cu, which is 5 to 10 times below the community-effective dose of 1 to 2 mg daily. The honest assessment: zero human combination trials exist. BPC-157 has one published human pilot (n=2, IV only) [2]. TB-500 has no human data at all for the subcutaneous route; the Phase I PK often cited (PMC8419156) studied recombinant full-length thymosin beta-4 given IV. GHK-Cu evidence is primarily in vitro and animal. Promising preclinical data and strong community consensus, but the clinical gap is real.

The GLOW Blend works through three distinct repair pathways that don't overlap. BPC-157 handles local, targeted repair. It upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) to drive angiogenesis at the injury site. New blood vessel formation accelerates nutrient delivery to damaged tissue. In isolated rat aorta, BPC-157 relaxed the vessel wall in a nitric oxide-dependent way, likely through Src-caveolin-1-eNOS signaling [7]. In rat tendon fibroblasts, it switched on FAK-paxillin signaling and sped cell migration [6]. A follow-up study found it raised growth hormone receptor expression in the same cell type [3]. TB-500 works systemically. As the active fragment of Thymosin Beta-4, it upregulates actin, a protein that enables cell migration and proliferation at wound sites. In Malinda's rat wound study, thymosin beta-4 raised reepithelialization over saline by 42% at day 4 and up to 61% at day 7 [4]. Kleinman and Sosne's 2016 review adds anti-inflammatory activity to its profile [5]. Both results come from full-length thymosin beta-4, not TB-500 itself. The plasma half-life usually cited for it, 0.5 to 2.08 hours, comes from a Phase I study of recombinant full-length thymosin beta-4 given intravenously (PMC8419156). That is a different molecule by a different route. No human dose-finding or PK data exists for subcutaneous TB-500. GHK-Cu adds the structural remodeling layer. This copper-binding tripeptide delivers copper ions directly to tissue, activating collagen I and III synthesis and promoting decorin expression. Decorin matters because it organizes collagen fibers into functional architecture rather than disorganized scar tissue. Pickart's group counts at least 4,000 human genes that GHK-Cu raises or lowers [1]. A 2015 review from the same group proposed that GHK-Cu acts on antioxidant-related genes, based on the Broad Institute's Connectivity Map gene-expression database (Cosmetics 2015). The three peptides clear plasma within hours. Structural and gene expression effects persist for weeks after clearance.
GLOW Blend benefits center on multi-pathway tissue repair, collagen remodeling, and systemic inflammation control.

Three-pathway healing in a single protocol: BPC-157 for local repair, TB-500 for systemic inflammation, GHK-Cu for structural collagen remodeling. No other peptide stack covers all three simultaneously.
Community users report higher-quality healed tissue versus the two-peptide Wolverine Stack, with less fibrotic scar formation (roughly 200+ Reddit threads, 4.3/5 sentiment).

GHK-Cu raises or lowers the activity of at least 4,000 human genes, including ones tied to tissue regeneration and antioxidant defense (Pickart) [1]. Skin firmness and elasticity improvements typically appear by week three to four.

Thymosin beta-4, TB-500's parent protein, raised reepithelialization in rat wounds 42% over saline at day 4 and up to 61% at day 7 [4]. A 2016 review also credits it with anti-inflammatory activity [5].
Single daily injection when using pre-mixed vials simplifies a three-peptide protocol into one subcutaneous dose, though separate vials allow better TB-500 frequency control.
Wound healing and skin texture improvements noted within three to six weeks across community reports; fine line reduction and scar softening peak at week six to eight.
Partially Aligned
Scientific Evidence
Based on 13 key studies · Research only
No combination studies exist for the three-peptide blend.

Dosing studied: Individual components only: no clinically validated combination dose. BPC-157: 250–500 mcg/day SC; TB-500: 2–5 mg twice weekly SC; GHK-Cu: 1–3 mg/day SC. Market-standard pre-mixed 70mg vial ratio: ~50mg GHK-Cu + 10mg BPC-157 + 10mg TB-500.

Individual components have preclinical (animal) support. BPC-157 has one published human IV safety pilot (n=2, 2025) [2]. TB-500 has no human data for the subcutaneous route; the Phase I PK cited for it (PMC8419156) studied recombinant full-length thymosin beta-4 given IV. GHK-Cu has gene-modulation in vitro data [1]. No RCTs for any component in the healing indications claimed.
Key Study

PMID 40131143 (2025 BPC-157 IV pilot, n=2, no adverse effects on cardiac/hepatic/renal/thyroid biomarkers); PMC12313605 (2025 systematic review BPC-157 orthopaedic sports medicine); PMID 26236730 (GHK-Cu raises or lowers at least 4,000 human genes, 2015 review); PMC8419156 (Phase I human PK of recombinant full-length thymosin beta-4 given IV, plasma t½ 0.5–2.08 hours: a different molecule and route from subcutaneous TB-500, for which no human dose-finding data exists)
Limitations

Zero human combination trials. BPC-157 pilot is n=2, uncontrolled, IV only (not SC). TB-500 human data is PK only: no efficacy endpoints. GHK-Cu data is primarily in vitro and animal. No dose-finding, safety, or efficacy RCTs for any component in humans.
Community Experience
Positive sentiment; users report meaningful healing quality improvement vs. BPC-157 + TB-500 alone, attributing collagen and skin/connective tissue benefits to GHK-Cu.

Community dosing: Market-standard 70mg vial (~2.33 mg total/injection in 3mL bac water = ~1.67mg GHK-Cu + 0.33mg TB-500 + 0.33mg BPC-157 daily). Separate-component protocol: BPC-157 500mcg/day + GHK-Cu 2mg/day + TB-500 2mg twice weekly (loading); halved for maintenance.
Primary concern: GHK-Cu underdosing in budget pre-mixed vials undermines outcomes.

b.x: Your first decision with this stack is vial format. Pre-mixed 70mg vials (typically 50mg GHK-Cu, 10mg BPC-157, 10mg TB-500) simplify everything into one daily draw. Separate component vials cost more time but let you dose TB-500 twice weekly (the community-preferred frequency) and avoid copper-catalyzed oxidation in a shared solution. Reconstitution math for the 70mg vial with 3 mL bacteriostatic water: concentration is 23.3 mg/mL, so one unit on a U-100 insulin syringe holds about 233 mcg. The beginner tier of 1,400 mcg is 6 units. Moderate (2,330 mcg) is 10 units. Aggressive (2,800 mcg) is 12 units. Do not carry over syringe unit calculations between vial formats. The thing most beginners miss: budget pre-mixed vials may contain only 200 mcg of GHK-Cu per dose. That is 5 to 10 times below the effective community dose. A blend's COA should list the exact milligrams of each component.
Cycling Protocol

Community cycles run 4 to 8 weeks depending on injury severity, 6 weeks most often, with a 2-week minimum break. The originating GLOW protocol sets no fixed length: it says to run until healing is achieved and take at least 15 days off between cycles. Neither schedule has trial support. For acute injuries 4 to 6 weeks is typical; some users extend to 8 weeks for chronic conditions with provider oversight.
GLOW Blend (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu) Continuous

No long-term combination safety data exists. Cycling limits cumulative copper load from GHK-Cu component and allows assessment of treatment response and adverse effects. GHK-Cu copper delivery is the primary driver: extended continuous use risks hepatic copper accumulation. The 4–8 week active / 2-week minimum off cycle is community consensus with no clinical trial basis for this specific combination. Receptor desensitization is sometimes given as the reason to cycle this stack. No desensitization data exists for BPC-157, TB-500, or GHK-Cu. The documented tachyphylaxis belongs to GH secretagogues, which are a different class and are not in this blend. Safety monitoring is the defensible reason to cycle; desensitization is not.

BPC-157 promotes angiogenesis via VEGFR2. That is the most serious safety concern in this stack. Anyone with active cancer or a history of cancer should not use GLOW. New blood vessel formation can theoretically feed tumor vasculature, and this risk is not theoretical enough to dismiss. BPC-157 directly antagonizes anti-angiogenic cancer therapies. GHK-Cu delivers exogenous copper systemically. Copper excess accumulates in the liver. Early signs include metallic taste, nausea, and abdominal discomfort. Users with Wilson's disease or any copper metabolism disorder have an absolute contraindication to this stack. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin testing at baseline is recommended, with repeat testing at week six for extended cycles or GHK-Cu doses above 2 mg daily. Target ranges: serum copper 70 to 140 mcg/dL, ceruloplasmin 20 to 40 mg/dL. TB-500 may affect clotting pathways. The interaction with anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) is unstudied in humans; theoretical bleeding risk exists. Unusual bruising or bleeding warrants immediate discontinuation. Injection site reactions are common across all three components. Redness, mild swelling, and irritation usually resolve within hours. GHK-Cu has a visible blue-teal tint from copper chelation. Mild discoloration at the injection site is normal and clears within 24 hours. Persistent swelling or redness points to insufficient site rotation. Community-reported side effects during week one include mild headache, occasional nausea, and lightheadedness. GHK-Cu may cause skin flushing on the first injection at higher doses. These typically resolve by week three. Human safety data is extremely limited. BPC-157 has one published pilot with two participants (IV route only) [2]. TB-500 human data covers pharmacokinetics only. GHK-Cu evidence is primarily in vitro and animal. The total number of humans formally studied on any component in this stack is under 50. When to stop: persistent headache lasting more than 48 hours; metallic taste or nausea that doesn't resolve; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of infection at the injection site; any active cancer diagnosis. When to see a doctor: copper excess symptoms, allergic reaction (hives or difficulty breathing), or any effect that feels wrong. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: do not use. No reproductive safety data exists for any component.
Common Issues & Solutions

No results by week 3: Verify GHK-Cu is adequately dosed. Budget pre-mixed vials may contain ~200 mcg GHK-Cu vs. the effective community dose of 1–2 mg. Check the COA for exact component mg breakdown; switch to separate vials if unverifiable.

Injection site turns bluish: GHK-Cu has a visible blue/teal tint due to copper chelation: mild discoloration at the injection site is normal and resolves within 24 hours. Persistent swelling or redness indicates insufficient site rotation.
Metallic taste or nausea after injection: Early indicator of copper sensitivity or mild copper excess from GHK-Cu. Reduce GHK-Cu dose by 50% for one week; discontinue if symptoms persist >48 hours.

No TB-500 effect: If using a pre-mixed daily vial, TB-500 is delivered in small daily fractions rather than the community-preferred 2×/week dosing. TB-500 tissue effects are dose-pulse–dependent in preclinical models: switch to separate vials for proper twice-weekly schedule.

Your vial ratio does not match 50/10/10: blend ratios are not standardized, and other splits are sold. The total mcg your calculator shows is still correct for any vial size you enter, but the per-component split on this page assumes 5:1:1 and will be wrong for a vial built to a different ratio. Read the COA, then work out the split from the milligram breakdown printed on it.

The 0.5-2 hour plasma half-life often quoted for TB-500 comes from a Phase I study of recombinant full-length thymosin beta-4 given intravenously (PMC8419156), not the subcutaneous heptapeptide sold as TB-500. BPC-157, TB-500, and GHK-Cu are sold as research compounds in the United States. None of the three components holds FDA approval for any therapeutic indication. The GLOW Blend combination has no regulatory status anywhere. These peptides are not approved drugs and are not legal for human therapeutic use outside of clinical research settings. BPC-157 and TB-500 are both explicitly prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA). Competitive athletes in any WADA-tested sport cannot use this stack. GHK-Cu is not currently on the WADA prohibited list. US compounding pharmacies have no legal pathway to prepare BPC-157 or TB-500. FDA lists both as withdrawn from its Category 2 list, but no FDA rule has added either to the 503A bulks list. Physician-supervised clinical sessions (IV or injection) run $200 to $400 per treatment at peptide clinics. Research-grade pre-mixed vials are sold online without prescription, though quality varies widely and no FDA oversight exists. This content is for educational and research purposes only. phases.notes: Start with separate vials for precise individual dosing. Do not use pre-mixed vials for first cycle: allows individual adjustment if side effects occur. Confirm no Wilson's disease or cancer history before starting.

protocols.monitoringNotes: Track any injection site reactions. Note any metallic taste (copper sensitivity). WADA caution: prohibited for competitive athletes. Not for use if cancer history or Wilson's disease.

faqs.a: The GLOW Blend combines BPC-157, TB-500, and GHK-Cu into a single healing-focused protocol. BPC-157 drives local repair through angiogenesis and growth factor expression. TB-500 promotes systemic cell migration. GHK-Cu raises or lowers the activity of at least 4,000 human genes, including ones related to tissue remodeling and copper-dependent repair enzymes.

faqs.q: What is the recommended GLOW Blend dosage?
faqs.a:
It depends on which product you have. A pre-blended 70 mg vial holds about 50 mg GHK-Cu, 10 mg BPC-157, and 10 mg TB-500, a 5:1:1 split fixed at manufacture. GHK-Cu is 71 percent of every draw, so the GHK-Cu dose sets the tier. A 1,400 mcg draw delivers 1,000 mcg GHK-Cu with 200 mcg each of BPC-157 and TB-500. A 2,330 mcg draw delivers about 1,670 / 330 / 330, which is the dose the originating protocol describes. A 2,800 mcg draw delivers 2,000 / 400 / 400. You cannot move one component without moving all three.

With separate vials you set each dose yourself. Community reports use GHK-Cu 2 mg per day, BPC-157 500 mcg per day, and TB-500 2 mg twice weekly. The originating protocol instead says to hold the 5:1:1 ratio when dosing separately. Those two do not agree and neither has trial support, so treat the choice as one to make with a prescriber.

Blend ratios vary. Check the COA before you calculate anything.

faqs.q: What are the side effects of the GLOW Blend?
faqs.a: Each component has minimal individual side effect profiles in community reports. The most common complaints are temporary brain fog, mild lethargy in the first week, and injection site soreness when combining multiple peptides. GHK-Cu can cause metallic taste at higher doses. Running three peptides simultaneously increases injection volume and frequency.

faqs.q: How long does the GLOW Blend take to work?
faqs.a: Community reports describe noticeable skin improvements from GHK-Cu within 2-3 weeks and soft tissue healing benefits from BPC-157 and TB-500 within 2-4 weeks. Community cycles run 4 to 8 weeks, 6 weeks most often. Hair and nail improvements from GHK-Cu typically require 4-8 weeks.

faqs.q: How do you reconstitute GLOW Blend (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu)?
faqs.a: GLOW Blend (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu) typically comes in 70mg vials. Add 3mL of bacteriostatic water to the vial. Use the free calculator for exact syringe units based on your desired dose. These totals apply to the pre-blended 70 mg vial, 5:1:1 GHK-Cu : BPC-157 : TB-500. Doses for separate component vials are set per component and are not the totals above. Ratios vary between products, so check the COA.

faqs.q: What is the half-life of GLOW Blend (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu)?
faqs.a: The half-life of GLOW Blend (BPC-157 + TB-500 + GHK-Cu) is Varies by component (~1-6 hours). This determines how frequently you need to dose for consistent blood levels.

summary: . Community users report smoother skin texture and faster injury recovery within three to six weeks. Zero combination trials exist in humans, and all clinical evidence comes from preclinical animal models or tiny pilot studies. Athletes recovering from soft tissue injuries and people chasing collagen density are the primary audience for this stack.
